walkthroughs.body_html:
Acidified K2Cr2O7 distilled off immediately -> aldehyde. Reflux -> carboxylic acid.

Colour change: orange Cr2O7^2- -> green Cr^3+. Secondary -> ketone (no further oxidation). Tertiary -> no reaction.

Tollens' reagent: Ag(NH3)2+ reduced to Ag (silver mirror) by aldehyde only.

Fehling's solution: blue Cu^2+ reduced to brick-red Cu2O by aldehyde only. Ketones do not react with either.

Carboxylic acid + alcohol with conc H2SO4 catalyst <-> ester + water (reversible).

Example: ethanoic acid + ethanol -> ethyl ethanoate + H2O. Excess alcohol shifts equilibrium right.

mcqs.q: What is the product of mild oxidation of a primary alcohol?
options: A primary alcohol is oxidised directly to a ketone.
An aldehyde (which can be further oxidised to a carboxylic acid).
A primary alcohol is oxidised to an alkene by losing water.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.

mcqs.q: What is reduction in terms of electrons?
options: Reduction means losing oxygen and oxidation means gaining oxygen — full stop.
The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.
Gain of electrons (the oxidation number is reduced).
Reduction means a substance becomes physically smaller in size.

mcqs.q: Is the oxidation state of an atom the same as its actual charge?
options: The oxidation state of an atom is always equal to the number of electrons it has.
Not necessarily — oxidation state is an accounting tool assuming all bonds are fully ionic; real charge is usually smaller.
The oxidation state of an atom is exactly equal to its real ionic charge in every compound.
Reduction means a substance becomes physically smaller in size.
